Expectation1: Listen actively and provide emotional support when needed.
Situation1: Your friend calls you in the middle of the night, crying, because they just received some devastating family news.
Expectation2: Arrive on time for scheduled volunteer shifts
Situation2: Several other volunteers can easily cover the first part of the shift if someone shows up a little late.
Story: My phone buzzed at 2 a.m., jolting me awake. It was Mia, her voice trembling as she told me her father had just been rushed to the hospital. She needed me—someone to listen, to help her hold together the pieces of her world. I sat up, heart pounding, trying to offer comfort, asking gentle questions, letting her cry. But as the minutes ticked by, I glanced at the clock. My volunteer shift at the shelter started at 6 a.m. sharp. I’d promised to be there on time, to help with the morning meal prep. I knew the others could cover for me if I was late, but I also knew how much reliability mattered to the team. My mind raced between Mia’s sobs and the image of the shelter kitchen, the expectation that I’d show up as promised. I wanted to be the friend Mia needed, but I also didn’t want to let down the people counting on me. The weight of both roles pressed on me, and I felt torn, unsure which responsibility should come first.
